books.title: The Yellow Wallpaper
books.author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
books.desc: Confined to an upstairs nursery for a "rest cure", a young mother becomes obsessed with the strange pattern of its yellow wallpaper.
about: A young woman spends the summer with her husband John, a physician, in a rented colonial mansion. Diagnosed with a "temporary nervous depression" after the birth of her baby, she is forbidden to work or write and is kept in a large room at the top of the house, with barred windows and a torn yellow wallpaper whose pattern disturbs her. Writing secretly in her journal, she describes how the wallpaper gradually takes over her thoughts.

Told in the first person, the story describes a woman's descent into madness and is a sharp criticism of the medical treatment of women and of a marriage in which the husband's authority leaves no room for the wife's own voice.

The Yellow Wallpaper was published in the New England Magazine in January 1892. It drew on Gilman's own experience of the "rest cure" prescribed to her in 1887 by the neurologist Silas Weir Mitchell. In her 1913 essay "Why I Wrote The Yellow Wallpaper", she explained that it was written "to save people from being driven crazy".

books.title: Bartleby, the Scrivener
books.author: Herman Melville
books.desc: A Wall Street lawyer hires a pale, quiet copyist who one day begins to answer every request with the words "I would prefer not to".
about: The narrator, an elderly and comfortable Wall Street lawyer, employs two eccentric copyists, Turkey and Nippers, and an office boy nicknamed Ginger Nut. When business grows, he hires a third scrivener, the pale and silent Bartleby, who at first copies documents tirelessly. Then one day, asked to check a copy, Bartleby calmly replies, "I would prefer not to", and his refusals gradually extend to everything.

Melville's story is at once comic and deeply sad. Its mysterious hero has been read in many ways, and the story raises questions about work, isolation, charity and the limits of understanding another person.
Bartleby, the Scrivener was first published anonymously in two parts in Putnam's Monthly Magazine in November and December 1853, and was included in Melville's collection The Piazza Tales in 1856.

books.title: Looking Backward: 2000–1887
books.author: Edward Bellamy
books.desc: A Bostonian falls into a hypnotic sleep in 1887 and wakes in the year 2000 to find a peaceful, cooperative society without poverty.
about: Julian West, a wealthy young Bostonian who suffers from insomnia, is put into a hypnotic sleep in a sealed underground chamber in 1887. He wakes in the year 2000 in the home of Dr Leete and his daughter Edith. The city around him has been transformed: industry is owned by the nation, every citizen serves in an "industrial army", goods are shared equally, and poverty, war and the conflict between capital and labour have disappeared. Dr Leete explains the new society to him.
Bellamy's novel uses a simple romantic story to present a detailed vision of a socialist utopia, and contrasts it with the inequalities and labour conflicts of the late nineteenth century.

Looking Backward was published in 1888 and became one of the best-selling American books of its century. It inspired a political movement, with many "Nationalist" clubs formed to discuss and promote its ideas, and a wave of utopian novels. Bellamy published a sequel, Equality, in 1897.
books.author_short: American author and journalist (1850–1898), whose utopian novel Looking Backward inspired a nationwide reform movement.
author_long: Edward Bellamy was born in Chicopee Falls, Massachusetts, on 26 March 1850. He trained in law but abandoned it in 1871, before he had properly begun to practise, and turned to journalism and fiction. He died of tuberculosis on 22 May 1898, aged 48.

After several novels and stories, he became famous with Looking Backward: 2000–1887 (1888), which led to the founding of many clubs devoted to its social and economic ideas. Its sequel, Equality, appeared in 1897.

books.title: The Pathfinder
books.author: James Fenimore Cooper
books.desc: On the shores of Lake Ontario during the French and Indian War, the frontiersman Natty Bumppo falls in love with a sergeant's daughter.
about: In the mid-eighteenth century, during the war between Britain and France for North America, Mabel Dunham travels through the forest with her uncle, the old sailor Charles Cap, to join her father, Sergeant Dunham, at a British fort near Oswego on Lake Ontario. They are guided by the scout Natty Bumppo, known as Pathfinder, his Mohican friend Chingachgook, and the young freshwater sailor Jasper Western. Pathfinder falls in love with Mabel, but the garrison faces danger and treachery on an expedition to the Thousand Islands.

The novel combines frontier adventure, sailing on the "inland sea" of Lake Ontario and a story of love and self-sacrifice. Its portrayal of Native Americans, including the Tuscarora Arrowhead and the "Mingo" enemies, relies on the stereotypes and vocabulary of its time.
The Pathfinder, or The Inland Sea was published in 1840. It is one of Cooper's five Leatherstocking Tales and the only one in which Natty Bumppo falls in love.

books.title: A Little Princess
books.author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
books.desc: A wealthy pupil at a London boarding school is suddenly left penniless and must work as a servant, but she never stops behaving like a princess.
about: Sara Crewe, brought up in India by her adoring father Captain Crewe, is sent to Miss Minchin's Select Seminary for Young Ladies in London, where she is treated as a show pupil. Imaginative and generous, she befriends the slow Ermengarde, little Lottie and Becky, the overworked scullery maid, and tells wonderful stories. When news comes that her father has died and his fortune has been lost, Miss Minchin sends Sara to live in a cold attic and to work as a servant, while a mysterious gentleman moves into the house next door.
Burnett's story celebrates imagination, kindness and dignity in hardship. Its picture of India and of the Indian servant Ram Dass reflects the colonial outlook of its time.

The story first appeared as the novella Sara Crewe, or What Happened at Miss Minchin's, serialised in St. Nicholas Magazine from December 1887 and published as a book in 1888. After turning it into a play in 1902, Burnett expanded it into the full novel A Little Princess, published in 1905.
